label: Preliminaries on Special Manifolds
notes: This opening chapter assembles the geometric vocabulary the whole book relies on. We meet the Stiefel manifold of orthonormal frames and the Grassmann manifold of subspaces, fix the orthogonal-group action that makes them homogeneous, and introduce the invariant measure that turns them into probability spaces.

label: The Stiefel Manifold
notes: The Stiefel manifold collects every orthonormal k-frame inside m-dimensional space, encoded as a tall matrix whose columns are mutually perpendicular unit vectors. The defining equation X transpose X equals the identity is a clean system of constraints that we will count carefully in a moment.

label: Counting Stiefel Dimensions
notes: Dimension counting subtracts constraints from the ambient coordinate count. A tall matrix has m times k entries, and orthonormality imposes k unit-length conditions plus the symmetric off-diagonal pairings. The bookkeeping yields the formula every later integral on the Stiefel manifold quietly assumes.

label: The Orthogonal Group Acts
notes: Left multiplication by an m by m orthogonal matrix rotates a frame into another frame while preserving every inner product. This action is transitive, so the Stiefel manifold is a single orbit, a homogeneous space, and the symmetry is the engine behind invariance arguments throughout the chapter.

label: The Grassmann Manifold
notes: The Grassmann manifold forgets which frame spans a subspace and remembers only the subspace itself. Each point is a k-dimensional plane through the origin, so a line through the origin in the plane is the smallest nontrivial example and fixes intuition for the higher cases.

label: Frames to Subspaces
notes: Two frames span the same subspace exactly when one is obtained from the other by a k by k orthogonal change of basis. Quotienting the Stiefel manifold by this right action of the smaller orthogonal group produces the Grassmann manifold as the space of orbits.

label: The Quotient Picture
notes: The quotient relation packages frames, subspaces, and rotations into one diagram. The Stiefel manifold sits above, the Grassmann manifold below, and the fibre over each subspace is a copy of the orthogonal group recording the frames that span it. Dimensions subtract cleanly across this map.

label: Invariant Measure
notes: Because the orthogonal group acts transitively, there is a unique probability measure invariant under that action, the normalized Haar measure. It is the only sensible notion of choosing a frame or a subspace uniformly at random, and it underwrites every distribution defined later.

label: Uniform Sampling
notes: A concrete recipe makes the invariant measure tangible. Fill a tall matrix with independent standard Gaussian entries and orthonormalize the columns; rotational symmetry of the Gaussian guarantees the resulting frame is uniform. The same draw projects down to a uniform random subspace on the Grassmannian.

label: Tangent Spaces
notes: Differentiating the constraint X transpose X equals identity along a curve shows the velocity must satisfy a skew-symmetry condition after projection. The tangent space splits into a horizontal part that moves the subspace and a vertical part that only spins the frame in place.

label: Exponential and Polar Coordinates
notes: Local coordinates make the manifolds computable. The matrix exponential of a skew-symmetric generator sweeps out geodesic-like curves, while the polar decomposition retracts any nearby full-rank matrix back onto the Stiefel manifold, giving two practical charts for analysis and simulation.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We now hold the core objects: Stiefel frames, Grassmann subspaces, their dimensions, the orthogonal-group symmetry, the invariant measure, and tangent coordinates. These preliminaries are the stage on which matrix-variate distributions, Frechet means, and asymptotic theorems are built in the chapters ahead.
